proposals.entity_key: Futur simple in narration (future from past standpoint)
value: English uses would, but French keeps the futur simple in this context
The conditional is used only when the future depends on a hypothesis, not in plain narration

evidence.notes: First entry comes from the stated English contrast; the second is the standard conditional/hypothesis distinction.

proposals.entity_key: Future in both clauses after certain conjunctions
value: English uses the present tense in the dependent clause, unlike French
The future is used in the dependent clause only after quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, and tant que, not after si

evidence.notes: First entry is the stated English contrast; the second follows from the listed conjunctions and the si rule.

value: The dependent clause is usually indicative, but the subjunctive appears when the main verb requires it
Indirect yes/no questions use si rather than que

evidence.notes: First entry qualifies the stated condition; the si for yes/no questions is standard grammar.

proposals.entity_key: Gerund expressing simultaneity, manner, condition, causality
value: The gerund shares the subject of the main clause and has no subject of its own
The meaning depends on context, so one sentence may allow several readings

evidence.notes: Both entries are standard grammar and match the rule's note about context.

value: The conditional never appears in the si clause
For past unreal conditions, si + plus-que-parfait with the past conditional is used instead

evidence.notes: First entry is the stated trap; the past-condition counterpart is standard grammar.

value: The reflexive pronoun must match the subject in person and number
In the affirmative imperative the pronoun follows the verb and becomes moi or toi
Some idiomatic pronominal verbs are neither reflexive nor reciprocal

evidence.notes: First entry is the stated agreement rule; the imperative and idiomatic exceptions are standard grammar.

value: Always impersonal: only il is used, never another subject
de becomes d' before a vowel (il s'agit d'un crime)
Il s'agit de + infinitive can also express necessity

evidence.notes: All three entries follow from the rule's fixed-expression status and listed usages.

value: Invariable: il y a serves both singular and plural (il y a un chat, il y a des chats)
In the negative, y is retained (il n'y a pas)
Il n'y a qu'à + infinitive is a fixed expression

evidence.notes: First two entries follow from the rule's formation and negative form; the third is a listed related expression.

value: Only aller serves as the auxiliary; no other verb forms this construction
The infinitive follows directly with no preposition
The present indicative of aller is required, not another tense

evidence.notes: First entry is the stated restriction; the absence of a preposition and the present-tense requirement come from the formation.

proposals.entity_key: Immediate future as substitute for future simple
value: The substitution is limited to colloquial and everyday speech, not formal writing
It expresses near future; a distant future keeps the futur simple

evidence.notes: First entry is the stated condition; the near-future limit is standard usage.
